ei.title: Scientific autonomy and political influence on research
ei.subject: 수능특강Light

fullPassage: Within the scientific community, few issues are more important than maintaining the independence of scientific researchers from external political or ideological influences. The current structure of peer review for funding decisions within research agencies, such as the National Science Foundation, is meant to allow a maximum of scientific autonomy within the confines of democratic accountability. Leading scientific spokespersons regularly proclaim the importance of autonomy and criticize the efforts of other political leaders to shape or change scientific and technological research priorities. However, with the pressures of shrinking research budgets, nonscience actors have begun to intrude directly into the research funding allocation processes through the "earmarking" of specific spending for science projects and facilities as riders to spending bills working through Congress. The specified projects often reflect the political influences of their sponsors, who often object that the traditional peer-reviewed processes seem too often to benefit certain well-known and well-endowed universities in certain states.

questions.passage: Within the scientific community, few issues are more important than maintaining the independence of scientific researchers from external political or ideological influences. The current structure of peer review for funding decisions within research agencies, such as the National Science Foundation, is meant to allow a maximum of scientific autonomy within the confines of democratic accountability. Leading scientific spokespersons regularly proclaim the importance of autonomy and criticize the efforts of other political leaders to shape or change scientific and technological research priorities. However, with the pressures of shrinking research budgets, nonscience actors have begun to intrude directly into the research funding allocation processes through the "earmarking" of specific spending for science projects and facilities as riders to spending bills working through Congress. The specified projects often reflect the political influences of their sponsors, who often object that the traditional peer-reviewed processes seem too often to benefit certain well-known and well-endowed universities in certain states.
